title: Beyond Interpretability: When, Why, and How Sparse Autoencoders Enable Label-Free Visual Steering
claim: A base method steers representations via sparse-feature deviation from a learned centroid, and a variant adds contrastive data to select features.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right, shared input cat image, subtraction and addition nodes merging into output
description: Two side-by-side pipeline diagrams, both starting with a cat photo fed into a frozen visual encoder (trapezoid with snowflake icon) that produces an embedding x, shown as a pink vertical bar. Panel (a), VS2, routes x through two parallel SAE encoder/decoder branches inside a dashed blue box labeled Contrastive-SAE. One branch reconstructs x. The other amplifies the sparse code by a factor gamma before decoding. The difference v is added to x with weight lambda, giving the steered output. Panel (b), VS2++, adds two dashed example groups: red positive images (cats) and blue negative images (other animals). Each group goes through the encoder and a Con-SAE, then is averaged to vp and vn. Their difference is added to x. Captions sit below each panel, and the red/blue color coding draws the eye first.
caption: Overview of \ours and \oursplus: \ours constructs a steering vector by uniformly amplifying active sparse features, while \oursplus selectively amplifies sparse features given external corpus.
abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) are increasingly used to interpret foundation models, but their role as an actionable intervention space remains less understood, especially in vision. We study whether sparse visual features can be used not only for post-hoc analysis, but also to steer frozen vision-language models. We introduce Visual Sparse Steering (VS2), a label-free method that trains a top-$k$ SAE on unlabeled activations from a frozen CLIP image encoder and, at test time, constructs an interpretable steering vector by amplifying the input's active sparse features and decoding the induced change. We show that this procedure admits a closed-form decomposition as centroid-deviation steering: each input is moved along its deviation from the SAE-learned centroid. The residual term is controlled exactly by the SAE's per-sample reconstruction error, measured by FVU, yielding an FVU-based residual bound and motivating a reliability gate that falls back to zero-shot CLIP when SAE reconstruction is unreliable. With target-domain SAEs trained on unlabeled CLIP image-encoder activations, VS2 improves zero-shot accuracy across nine image-classification datasets, achieving gains up to $+4.12\%$ with less than $0.1\%$ additional inference compute. Finally, a controlled upper-bound study, VS2++, shows that selective amplification of sparse features can yield gains up to $+21.44\%$, exposing a reconstruction-vs-task saliency gap: features salient for reconstruction need not align with features useful for downstream prediction.
